text:
Toledo is an ecclesiastical city.

For a single night of the year,

its household vines

give a clear wine.


A little wine that reddens the palate

of the eponymous marzipan,

and very gently prepares one

to receive into the soul the canonical aroma

of black grapes in brandy.


For the Church

allows gluttony:

for every craving there is a license;

for every sweet, a papal bull.


And candid sugar drips

through the transparency of the Cathedral;

and in her arms the Virgin cradles

the little edible god,

pink and salmon;

and oh, what famous slices of the Alcázar,

if, being granite, they were nougat!


For the Church allows gluttony;

and I know a nun who is all sugar.

And who keeps heaven addicted

to honey spun through her hair,

and knows how to make walnut electuaries,

and others of bitter-root carrots,

and citron, codonate, and rosetta,

and Alexandrian cumin sweet,

and so many other things I could not finish.


But that confectioner—where was he—

who made the holy mysteries

in sugar, almond, and cinnamon?

Pentecost and the Trinity,

Corpus and the Ascension,

and a Jesus almost true

with a little almond in his heart.


But art has its rules,

and each figure its share.

And there was also a Lucifer

with a sour, elongated face,

and he put in his heart

an unusual bitter almond.


Terror of mothers: hidden death

in the sweets!

Seasoning by the handful,

with the verdigris of kitchens!


I know well that art has its rules,

and each figure gets its share.

But to sugar-coat bitter almonds,

even if they are the heart's?

Unneeded charities,

I swear they are.


To disguise a Lucifer cunningly,

so that he is mistaken for a Savior?

Unneeded charities,

I swear they are.


Oh, good maker!

There is better art:

do not sell me rancor in syrup,

if I am to find gall

in the heart.

translation.title: The Bad Confectioner
translation.editorial_note: The source contains the marked phrase “aroma Canonical”; it is retained as “canonical aroma” rather than silently normalized. Rare confection names are transliterated or rendered descriptively.
